name: Grounds for Thought: Janpath
description: Grounds for Thought: Janpath, September 2026A Blue Tokai × unLecture Series, Three Tuesday evenings. Three very different conversations.Grounds for Thought is a monthly series where Blue Tokai and unLecture bring researchers, scientists, and thinkers out of their institutions and into a coffee shop. The format is simple: an expert, a room full of curious people, and a conversation that goes somewhere a classroom rarely does. This September, the series spreads further than ever — four venues across Delhi and Bangalore, and a spread of ideas running from gender and work to princely politics, from children's books to comic-book uncles.17th September: Prateek MundejaWhy Do Good Ideas Fail in Government?Governance is usually discussed in ideals — promises, ambition, the world as it ought to be. Prateek Mundeja, Assistant Professor of Political Science and Mookerjee Fellow (2025–26), argues that the more useful question is a duller one: what actually works? This session takes a realist's tour through limited resources, institutional capacity, and the gap between stated intentions and delivered outcomes — and makes the case that ideals only survive contact with the world when backed by hard, unglamorous choices.29th September: Amitrajeet MukherjeeVoices from War: Revisiting John Keegan's The Face of BattleJohn Keegan's landmark book opened with a deceptively simple question — what is it actually like to be in a battle? Fifty years on, his witnesses remain almost entirely European, despite spanning centuries of warfare. Amitrajeet Mukherjee, a doctoral candidate in English Literature at Delhi University, widens that frame to the two and a half million Indians who served in the Second World War — diarists, letter-writers, the censored and the unrecorded — and asks whose voices get to define what "war writing" is for.

name: When AI Starts Inventing
description: When AI Starts Inventing: How AI Is Cracking Problems That Have Resisted Us for Decades, and How to Bring It from Big Tech's Labs to Your LaptopIn September 2026, OpenAI announced that a team of AI agents had produced a proof, machine-verified in Lean, for a problem about how fluids move that has stood open for ninety years and carries a million-dollar prize. Before that, an AI agent found a faster way to multiply matrices, the operation that sits underneath almost all modern computing, beating a record set in 1969. It is starting to feel routine: every few weeks, another problem that resisted people for decades quietly falls to an AI agent.How does this actually happen? That is what we will look at first, because the mechanism turns out to be stranger and simpler than most people expect.Then a harder question. Every time the agent is asked to produce something, someone pays, and the more capable the AI, the higher the bill. A single discovery run makes thousands of such calls, which is why almost all of this work happens inside a handful of enormously wealthy labs. In our lab we are trying to change that, and doing so means asking questions nobody bothers to ask when the budget is unlimited. Does every step really need the most expensive AI model, or would a cheaper one do just as well? Is every attempt the agent makes actually worth making? Our investigation of these discovery pipelines, across several notoriously hard problems, reveals that around 98% of the AI agent's calls contribute nothing to the eventual solution. And they still succeed. Which leaves a genuinely open question: is that waste the price of discovery, or simply a bill nobody has bothered to reduce?About the SpeakerProf. Sayan Ranu is the DS Chair Professor in AI at IIT Delhi, jointly appointed in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering and the Yardi School of AI. His research focuses on machine learning for structured data, particularly graphs, and increasingly on AI systems that can reason, plan and discover solutions on their own. His work spans automated algorithm discovery, AI agents, self-supervised learning and trustworthy AI. His research has been published at leading AI and machine learning conferences including NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR and KDD. He was also a recipient of the Teaching Excellence Award at IIT Delhi and currently serves as a Senior Area Chair for NeurIPS 2026 and Program Co-Chair for the Datasets & Benchmarks Track at KDD 2027.Book now & develop your own pint of view! 🍻

name: Rewriting Epics The Feminist Way
description: About the LectureThe Epics have held the Indian imagination since time immemorial, narrated, performed and rendered into cinema again and again. Looking at them afresh means asking the questions they've spent centuries deflecting: the role of women, the contribution of the dispossessed, and the quintessential human questions of survival and existence.A feminist retelling brings the women back to the centre. It strips away the proverbial sheen of the "just" war to focus on the human question underneath. Whether it's the fiery Draupadi, the "manipulative" Satyavati, the warrior queen Chitrangada, Janaki, or the duo of Kaikeyi and Manthara, the Epics allow us to deconstruct these women through a modern feminist lens.The session explores:How feminist retellings of the Mahabharata and Ramayana recentre their women charactersWhat writers like Tagore, Mahasweta Devi, Irawati Karve and Chitra Divakaruni reveal through their retellingsWhy the Epics' "timeless" characters remain contemporary and urgently relevantHow deconstructing canonical narratives changes what the stories are actually aboutAbout the SpeakerDr. Nandini C. Sen is a Professor of English at the University of Delhi — an author, editor, literary critic and storyteller. For nearly three decades, she has explored how literature shapes the way we understand history, identity, gender and the world around us, working across African Literature, Diaspora studies, mythology, postcolonial studies and feminist readings of the Indian epics. Her academic journey has taken her from Delhi to London as a Charles Wallace Scholar, to the Indian Institute of Advanced Study, Shimla as a Fellow, and to universities and literary forums across the world. She is the recipient of the Write India Award for creative writing, the Ambassador for Peace Prize for teaching in a slum cluster, and the Best Lecturer's Award from the Government of Delhi. She is the author of the bestselling short story collection The Second Wife and Other Stories, and editor of several acclaimed books.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Nani's Table by V's Supper Stories
description: Nani ka Ghar by V's Supper Stories A supper brunch of home-cooked nostalgia.Some recipes don't survive migration. They get left behind in old kitchens, remembered only in fragments- a smell, a story, a dish someone's grandmother used to make that no one quite knows how to recreate anymore.Nani ka Ghar is a supper built around dishes like that. Rooted in Multan, where my own Nani is from, and reaching into Lahore and Sindh - the homes our grandparents carried with them. This menu brings back food that's slow, laborious, and increasingly rare: a sourdough flatbread fermented over three days, a lotus-stem starter barely made anymore even in Sindhi households, a moth dal kachori you'll mostly only find on a handful of old Delhi streets.Alongside them sit the dishes that never left, a rich Lahori chicken karahi, a comforting channay, and phirni made exactly the way it's made every Holi in our family, because some things don't need reviving. They just need to be shared.Come hungry. Come with stories of your own kitchens, if you have them.Date - 4th October Time - 12:30pm - 3pmA limited seating supper. name: Lucia's Student Showcase 2026 | The Rising Stars
description: Sentirenla Lucia is a vocalist, vocal coach and performing artist specializing in R&B, Neo-soul and Contemporary Jazz. Originally from Nagaland and Kerala, India, she draws on her diverse cultural heritage and deep roots in gospel, choral and contemporary music.Based in New Delhi since 2016, Lucia teaches private voice and has worked with The British School, Global Music Institute and Blue Notes School of Music in the Delhi NCR region. She works with singers focusing on healthy vocal technique, musicality, confidence and individual expression. She continues to perform whenever the opportunity arises. Many students that she has mentored have been accepted into prestigious Music Colleges such as Berklee College of Music, Oberlin Conservatory of Music, BIMM etc. with scholarship under her tutelage.Lucia began performing and recording professionally in New Delhi, working on jingles and television projects that received nationwide radio and television airplay. In 2002, she became a founding member of Artistes Unlimited, a 60-member choir and charitable trust, collaborating with artists including Shubha Mudgal, Parikrama and composer Julius Packiam. She has also performed with Them Clones and other leading musicians.In 2005, Lucia received a scholarship through Berklee College of Music’s World Scholarship Tour. She graduated from Berklee in 2010 with a degree in Vocal Performance. During her time there, she performed at the Berklee Performance Center, sang background vocals for artists including Tata Vega, Rhiannon and Larry Watson, and shared stages with Lalah Hathaway, Amel Larrieux, Esperanza Spalding and Eguie Castrillo. She also worked as a session vocalist and was selected to sing in a tribute to Angelique Kidjo at Berklee’s graduation ceremony.Lucia has taught and performed in both India and the United States. In Boston, she taught private voice and directed a cappella ensembles at Zumix, City Music – Berklee College of Music and School of Groove. She has also performed with Jazz Urbane, Semper Soul, The Singing Tribe and Sung Deep, and founded Phoenix Anthology to promote musical diversity and create opportunities for musicians from Nagaland. After she received her Artist Visa she taught private voice lessons and background. She also had the privilege to attend a workshop with Bobby McFerrin, who is her inspiration and since then has been on the journey to discover every aspect of vocal training attainable.Lucia hopes to inspire and motivate those who may have lost their sense of purpose through music, while continuing to learn, perform and contribute to a more diverse and expressive musical community.

name: Body Language Speaks Louder Than Words
description: About the LectureA raised eyebrow. A shift in posture. A half-second pause before an answer. Long before you finish a sentence, your body has usually already told the room the truth.This lecture explores body language as one of the most powerful forms of communication we have. From micro-expressions and eye movements to posture, gestures and the subtle inconsistencies between what someone says and what they do, we'll examine how non-verbal cues reveal emotion, confidence, stress and intention long before words catch up.Drawing on years of training law enforcement, forensic and academic institutions across India — from the Delhi Police Crime Branch to CISF and the CBI's forensic science laboratory — and on his recent analysis of world leaders at the BRICS Summit in New Delhi, Gaurav Gill takes the same tools used in interrogation rooms and diplomatic summits and turns them toward everyday life: negotiations, dates, interviews, and the conversations you have every day without realising how much you're saying.The session explores:How facial expressions, posture and gestures reveal what words often hideThe difference between a nervous habit and a genuine sign of deceptionHow law enforcement and forensic experts read non-verbal cues in real investigationsPractical ways to apply body language reading to your own personal and professional lifeAbout the SpeakerGaurav Gill is a body language expert and consultant psychologist who has trained several of India's most prestigious law enforcement, forensic and academic institutions. In September 2026, WION News invited him to analyse the non-verbal communication of global leaders at the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi, decoding the handshakes, gestures, posture, facial expressions, eye contact and physical proximity behind high-level diplomatic engagements. He has also featured on Raj Shamani's Figuring Out podcast, in an episode that has drawn more than 2.9 million views.His training assignments include the Delhi Police Crime Branch AHTU, Delhi Police (Central District — Kamla Market, Hauz Khas and IP Estate), Pune Police and Pune Crime Branch AHTU, SPUWAC Headquarters (Special Police Unit for Women and Children), the Railway Protection Force (RPF), Government Railway Police (GRP), CISF and the CISF ASG Unit. He has conducted specialised body language training for forensic experts at DFSS-CFSL (formerly CBI-CFSL), New Delhi, and has been guest faculty at the National Forensic Sciences University (Delhi and Goa campuses), Rashtriya Raksha University (Gujarat campus) and the Juvenile Justice Board (JJB-VII), Dwarka, Delhi.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. description: About the LectureWe sometimes just think of pots as functional. But across three cultures — Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan — the same simple act of shaping wet clay reveals three completely different value systems: community and belonging, beauty and craftsmanship, imperfection and impermanence.This talk isn't really about pottery. It's about how to read the objects around us, and what your own everyday things might be quietly saying about you.Drawing on folklorist Henry Glassie's The Potter's Art, the session zooms into three pottery traditions: in Bangladesh, pottery woven into caste, community and everyday ritual life; in Turkey, pottery as a vessel for aesthetic pride and decorative mastery; and in Japan's Hagi tradition, tied to the tea ceremony, where the values invert entirely — imperfection, asymmetry and impermanence, the wabi-sabi aesthetic, are not flaws to correct but the entire point.The session explores:How the same craft, shaping wet clay, produces radically different worlds of meaning across culturesWhat pottery in Bangladesh, Turkey and Japan reveals about caste, beauty and impermanenceWhy folk art is never really anonymous, static or purely functionalWhat your own everyday objects might be quietly saying about what you valueAbout the Speaker Simran Sushila is a folklorist and a professor, currently pursuing her PhD in Folklore at Indiana University Bloomington, USA. Her research looks at how communities use tradition to make sense of identity, memory, belonging, and change....and then, somewhere along the way, the she became an entrepreneur. Years of teaching and evaluating students made her increasingly curious about something: how does a person take what they know – and make another person see it, understand it, and believe it?That question became The VoiceCraft Institute: her attempt to build something India doesn't quite have yet – a serious space for learning expression, language, and communication, beyond grammar classes and beyond test-prep English.Because knowing English is one thing. Knowing what to say, how to say it, and how to make it land – that's a craft. And crafts can be taught.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. Created by three friends from college who wanted learning to feel warm, social and alive — unLecture turns an otherwise ordinary evening into a conversation you may think about long after it ends.

name: Designing Your Life, The Stanford Way
description: About the LectureWhat if the life you're living right now is one you drifted into by default, not one you chose?We are born into stories, about success, work, money, relationships, identity and what a good life should look like. Somewhere along the way, those stories start to feel like our own, and a life shaped by default begins to feel like one shaped by choice.Stanford's Designing Your Life offers another way to look at it: life as something you can actively design. That doesn't mean finding one "true" self or one perfect path. It means moving towards self-authorship: questioning the narratives you inherited, imagining different futures, and accepting that there may be more than one life within you worth living.Design turns out to be an unusually useful lens for this, because it doesn't require you to know the answer before you begin. It lets you work with ambiguity, hold several possibilities at once, and experiment rather than predict. In a world where lives are increasingly nonlinear, that may be more useful than having a perfect plan.The session explores:How inherited social narratives quietly become the stories we live byWhy there may be more than one life within us worth livingHow designers work with ambiguity, and why that matters for life decisionsMoving from a life by default to a life by design: question, imagine, prototypeAbout the SpeakerNavyug Mohnot is a Stanford-certified Designing Your Life educator, coach and facilitator, a visiting faculty member at ISB and Ashoka University, and the founder and CEO of QAI Global. He is a certified leadership coach from Harvard University, has spoken at conferences around the world, and is a TEDx speaker ("Manifesting Desires, Embracing Contradictions"). He has coached professionals across the globe, served on company boards, and mentored startups as an angel investor. Navyug did his B.Tech at IIT Delhi and received the "Outstanding Contribution to National Development" award from the IIT Delhi Alumni Association. Outside work, he meditates, runs a film club, loves art, film and architecture, and hopes to direct a full-length film someday.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Clearing the Smoke and Mirrors
description: About the LectureJoin us for a lecture that cuts through the winter blame game:Delhi blames Punjab, Punjab blames Delhi, and everyone blames the weather. So what is actually in the air we breathe?We've all been there: complaining about the AQI, feeling what the air does to our lungs, sleep, skin and routines. Every winter we're handed the same list of culprits: stubble burning, construction dust, industrial emissions, cars, trucks, garbage fires, landfills, brick kilns, diesel generators and, of course, the wind. The panels shout, the season passes, and by next November we're no clearer on which of these actually matters, or by how much.Atmospheric scientist Dr Mohammad Rafiuddin begins with Delhi's meteorology and geography: a landlocked city on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, hemmed in by the Himalayas, with winter air that sits still. It's a bad hand, but not a unique one, and if cities around the world with the same conditions have got their air under control, so can Delhi. From there, we'll go sector by sector through what's actually in the air, and which solutions would genuinely cut emissions from each.The session explores:Why Delhi's geography and winter weather trap pollution, and why that isn't an excuseWhat's actually in Delhi's air: transport, biomass and solid-fuel burning, waste, dust, construction, industry and stubbleWhich sources matter most, and by how muchThe solutions that would genuinely cut emissions, sector by sectorAbout the SpeakerDr Mohammad Rafiuddin is an atmospheric scientist who once built a fog-forecasting system for Bengaluru airport, which means pilots have landed on his maths. He is now Programme Lead – Clean Air at CEEW, where he researches what Delhi's air is made of, how well the city can predict it, and why the answer never stops at Delhi's border. He holds a PhD in atmospheric sciences from the Jawaharlal Nehru Centre for Advanced Scientific Research, Bengaluru, a Post Graduate Diploma in Urban Environmental Management and Law from National Law University, and a BTech in mechanical engineering from Jawaharlal Nehru Technological University, Hyderabad.About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Tales of Indigenous Indian Entrepreneurship
description: About the LectureLong before Zomato and Zerodha, who was building India's wealth, and how?Indian entrepreneurship is strangely under-represented in the mainstream story. Startup India and the unicorns tipped the balance a little, but India's business history goes back hundreds of years before the "Z brothers" became household names. Indian traders and entrepreneurs were building financial instruments, credit systems, accounting methods and contract management long before these were written up in Harvard textbooks and case studies.Most of us know almost nothing about this history. Many of the communities that built it have faded into obscurity, with tales of a glorious past but rarely a shared plan for the future. This lecture digs into what made them great, what they invented, and what happened to that edge.The session explores:What made India's traditional business communities so successfulThe innovations in business and finance that built the wealth of the Jagat Seths, the Birlas and everyone who came afterMarwari social and cultural systems, and how they shaped individual and collective entrepreneurshipThe lost edge, and whether there's hope for the futureAbout the SpeakerDr Nihar Amoncar is Pro Vice Chancellor at IILM University and Director of the IILM School of Management. He completed his PhD in Family Business Strategy on a full scholarship at the University of South Wales, and has won several international awards for his research on traditional business communities, including the Best Paper Award at the Academy of Marketing. He is a Fellow of Higher Education (UK), serves on the board of the Academy of Marketing's Special Interest Group on Entrepreneurship and Marketing, and is the Asia representative of GRCME (USA).About unLectureunLecture brings experts out of classrooms and into cafés, bars and neighbourhood spaces across Delhi. name: Can We Make Delhi a Human City?
description: Welcome to Human City Conversations where we have intimate conversations about how cities are built, how they are lived, and who gets to shape them.Conversation 1: HOW DO WE MAKE DELHI A HUMAN CITY?Delhi is a city of contradictions. It has some of India's best public institutions, an expanding metro network, enormous infrastructure projects and a new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 that sets out a vision for how the city should grow and change over the next two decades. And yet, the experience of living in Delhi can be very different.Millions of people spend hours commuting across the city. Walking can feel like an afterthought. Public spaces are often unevenly distributed and poorly connected. For many women, moving through the city comes with a calculation of safety that men may never have to make. And then there is the air. Every winter, Delhi's air pollution becomes a public health crisis forcing a city of millions to think about something as fundamental as whether it is safe to breathe outside.So how can a city with so much planning, infrastructure and investment still struggle with some of the most basic conditions of everyday urban life? Perhaps the problem is not simply how much we build, perhaps we need to ask a more fundamental question:What kind of city are we actually trying to build? And more importantly, who is that city being built for?For the first Human City Conversation, urbanist Jagan Shah joins Ruchita Bansal for an open conversation about Delhi, its future and the gap between the city we plan on paper and the city people actually experience. We'll explore what makes a city genuinely liveable from mobility and housing to public space, safety, air pollution and neighbourhoods and look at what Delhi's new Master Plan for 2047 could mean on the ground.What to ExpectA curated, open conversation between urbanist Jagan Shah and Ruchita BansalA look at Delhi's urban future and what the new Master Plan for Delhi 2047 could mean on the groundA discussion about the gap between the city we plan and the city people actually experienceA closer look at how cities are shaped by policies, infrastructure and development decisionsPerspectives on what makes a city genuinely liveable, accessible and inclusiveA 30 minute Q&A SessionInformal discussion and one on one conversation after the conversationEvent Details📅 Sunday, 11 October 2026🕔 5:00 PM onwards📍 Kunzum Books, GK II, Delhi☕ Your ticket includes one coffee/tea .About the SpeakerJagan Shah is an urbanist, architect and former Director of the National Institute of Urban Affairs (NIUA), with decades of experience working at the intersection of urban planning, policy, governance and development. He has been closely involved in shaping India's urban policy and planning landscape, including work connected to Delhi's Master Plan, the Smart Cities Mission and other national urban development programmes. His work has involved developing and implementing policies and frameworks that influence how Indian cities grow, transform and respond to the challenges of rapid urbanisation.Over the years, Jagan has worked across urban planning, housing, infrastructure, heritage, governance and institutional development, working with governments and institutions at different levels.His experience spans both the making of plans and policies and the realities of implementing them, making him particularly well placed to examine the gap between the city we envision on paper and the city that people actually experience.About the ModeratorRuchita Bansal is an architect and urban planner with 15 years of experience working on cities, urban development and planning policy. Her work has ranged from developing planning frameworks and regulations to working directly on large-scale urban transformation projects. She was part of the team behind Ayodhya Vision 2047, working on one of India's most complex and rapidly transforming urban environments and seeing first-hand the challenges of translating ambitious plans and visions into reality on the ground.Today, Ruchita is the Creator and Host of The Human City Podcast and the founder of SheCity India, using conversations, research and storytelling to make urban planning more accessible and bring the discussion about cities beyond the professional planning community. Through The Human City, she explores a simple but often overlooked question: what does all this planning mean for the people who actually live in our cities?Note: Attendance implies consent to being filmed for event documentation. If you do not wish to be filmed, please reach out to your curator for the evening, Ruchita. Come curious. Come questioning. Come ready to talk about the city we call home.
